title: The atomic nucleus and radioactivity
summary: Learn about the nucleus, binding energy, α, β and γ radiation, half-life, fission and fusion.
cards.0.p: The protons and neutrons in a nucleus are called nucleons. Z is the number of protons and A is the number of nucleons, so N = A − Z. Nuclei with the same Z but different A are called isotopes. 12C and 14C are an example.
cards.0.key: Z decides the element. If A changes you get an isotope, and if Z changes you get a different element.
cards.1.p: The force that holds the protons together is called the strong nuclear force. It acts between all nucleons, whatever their charge. Its range is very short. At about 1 fm it beats the repulsion, and a little farther out it drops to zero.
cards.1.key: 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neutrons add attraction without adding repulsion. That is why they matter for the stability of the nucleus.
cards.2.p: The mass of a nucleus is slightly less than the total mass of its nucleons. This difference is called the mass defect (Δm). When the nucleus forms, this mass is released as an energy of E = Δm·c². This energy is called the binding energy.
cards.2.key: To break the nucleus into its parts, you must supply the same energy. A mass defect of 1 u corresponds to about 931.5 MeV.
cards.3.p: The ratio of binding energy to nucleon number shows how tightly a nucleus is bound. The curve peaks around A ≈ 56-62 (about 8.8 MeV). For heavy nuclei it falls slowly.
cards.3.svg#7: moving toward the peak gives energy
cards.3.key: Light nuclei move toward the peak by joining, and heavy nuclei by splitting. Energy is released along the way.
cards.4.p: Alpha (α) radiation is a helium nucleus. In β⁻ decay a neutron turns into a proton, and in β⁺ decay a proton turns into a neutron. Gamma (γ) is a high-energy photon, and gamma emission does not change the element.
cards.4.key: β⁻ gives an electron and an antineutrino. β⁺ gives a positron (a positively charged antielectron) and a neutrino.
cards.4.etk.soru: Match each decay with the change it makes in the nucleus.
cards.4.once.soru: A nucleus emits alpha radiation. What comes out?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: An electron comes out in β⁻ decay.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: A high-energy photon is gamma radiation.
cards.5.p: In light, stable nuclei N/Z ≈ 1. Heavy nuclei need more neutrons to balance the repulsion of the protons, and the ratio approaches 1.5. All nuclei heavier than lead are radioactive.
cards.5.key: A nucleus with too many neutrons undergoes β⁻, and one with too many protons β⁺. Very heavy nuclei usually undergo α.
cards.5.once.soru: What does a nucleus with too many neutrons do to become stable?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.yazi: Turns a neutron into a proton
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: With β⁻ decay, N goes down and Z goes up. This fixes the ratio.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: Absorbing a neutron makes the excess larger.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: Gamma emission does not change N or Z. It only gets rid of energy.
cards.6.h: A and Z are conserved in the equation
cards.6.p: In a decay equation, the total A and the total Z are equal on both sides. α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ decay raises Z by 1. You find the number of α from the difference in A first, then the number of β from Z.
cards.6.svg#14: Z: 90 − 12 = 78;  4 β⁻ to get up to 82
cards.6.key: Going from ²³²Th down to ²⁰⁸Pb takes 6 α and 4 β⁻. β and γ emissions do not change A.
cards.7.h: Penetration and deflection in an electric field
cards.7.p: α radiation is stopped by paper, and β radiation by aluminum. γ is the most penetrating. In a magnetic field α and β⁻ bend in opposite directions, and the lighter β bends more. γ does not bend.
cards.7.key: The order of penetration is γ > β > α. The order of ionizing power is the reverse: α > β > γ. Lead only weakens γ radiation.
cards.8.p: The time it takes for half of the nuclei to decay is called the half-life (T½). With n = t / T½, the amount left is N = N₀ / 2n.
cards.8.key: From 80 g of a substance with a half-life of 5 days, 10 g is left after 15 days. After 2 half-lives the substance is not gone: a quarter is left. Half-life does not change with temperature.
cards.8.etk.soru: Change the starting amount, the half-life and the time passed: N = N<sub>0</sub> / 2<sup>t/T½</sup>.
cards.9.p: When a living thing dies, it stops taking in new <sup>14</sup>C. The <sup>14</sup>C it has decreases with a half-life of about 5730 years. If the <sup>14</sup>C/<sup>12</sup>C ratio has dropped to a quarter, about 11 460 years have passed.
cards.9.svg#0: fraction of ¹⁴C left after death
cards.9.key: While alive, the ratio is close to that of the atmosphere. The method is reliable only for samples that were once alive, up to ≈50 000 years.
cards.9.once.soru: In a bone, the ¹⁴C ratio is half that of a living thing. The half-life is 5730 years. How old is the bone?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: The ratio has halved once. That means one half-life.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: That is two half-lives, and the ratio would have dropped to a quarter.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Dropping to half takes one full half-life.
cards.10.p: In fission a heavy nucleus such as 235U absorbs a neutron, splits and releases 2-3 neutrons. These neutrons start a chain reaction. In fusion, light nuclei join. Both release energy.
cards.10.svg#11: in the core of the Sun
cards.10.key: Nuclear power plants run fission under control. The Sun turns hydrogen into helium. Fusion needs temperatures of millions of kelvins.
cards.11.p: Radiation is used in medicine for imaging and tumor treatment, in food preservation and in industry. Irradiated food does not become radioactive. To protect yourself, stay a short time, keep away and put shielding in between.
cards.11.key: Instruments are sterilized with radiation, and welds are checked for flaws. Doubling your distance from a point source cuts the radiation to about a quarter.
cards.11.once.soru: Do strawberries preserved by irradiation become radioactive?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: The radiation kills microbes but adds no radioactive material to the strawberries.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Being irradiated is not the same as being contaminated with radioactive material.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: When the beam stops, its effect ends, and the strawberries do not radiate.
cards.12.p: The number of decays per second is called activity, and its unit is the becquerel (Bq). A person who is irradiated does not become radioactive. If radioactive material gets on or into the body, that is contamination.
cards.12.key: Activity halves with every half-life. Dose is measured in grays (Gy), and biological effect in sieverts (Sv).
cards.12.once.soru: Does someone who had an X-ray taken give off radiation afterward?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: A person who is irradiated does not become radioactive.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: X-rays do not stay in the body.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: There is no radiation unless radioactive material enters the body.
cards.13.p: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks. The u quark has charge +2/3 and the d quark −1/3. A proton is made of uud and a neutron of udd. The electron and the neutrino are leptons, which as far as we know cannot be split.
cards.13.svg#10: leptons: electron, muon, tau and neutrinos
cards.13.key: In β⁻ decay, a d quark actually turns into a u. Quarks are never found alone.
cards.13.once.soru: A proton is made of uud quarks (u: +2/3, d: −1/3). What is its total charge?
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: 0 is the charge of the neutron (udd).
cards.13.once.secenekler.2.neden: The d quark is negatively charged: 4/3 − 1/3 = 1.
cards.14.p: There are four fundamental forces: the strong, electromagnetic, weak and gravitational force. The weak force governs β decay. The forces are carried by gluons, photons, and W and Z bosons. The graviton has not been observed yet.
cards.14.key: Every particle has an antiparticle. The antiparticle of the electron is the positron. The photon is its own antiparticle.
cards.14.once.soru: Which force holds the nucleus together?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: The strong force has a short range, but it is very strong. So it beats the repulsion of the protons.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: At the scale of the nucleus, gravity is almost negligibly weak.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: The electromagnetic force pushes the protons apart.
cards.15.p:
• Z is the number of protons, A−Z the number of neutrons.
• The strong force has a short range.
• E = Δm·c², and nuclei near iron are the most stable.
• α: A−4, Z−2. β⁻: Z+1, β⁺: Z−1.
• N = N₀/2ⁿ, and ¹⁴C gives the age.
• Fission and fusion release energy.
quiz.0.q: How many grams of 64 g of a radioactive substance with a half-life of 2 hours remain undecayed after 8 hours?
quiz.0.e: n = 8/2 = 4 half-lives pass. The amount left is 64/2<sup>4</sup> = 4 g.
quiz.1.q: Put each property with the radiation it belongs to.
quiz.1.e: Alpha is a helium nucleus. It is stopped by paper and lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. Beta minus is an electron. It raises Z by 1 and bends toward the positive plate. Gamma is an uncharged photon. It is not deflected and does not change A or Z.
quiz.2.q: According to the curve of binding energy per nucleon, does each reaction give energy or need energy?
quiz.2.e: The peak of the curve is around iron. Reactions that move toward the peak give energy. The fusion of light nuclei and the fission of heavy nuclei are examples. Splitting or fusing iron, which is at the peak, needs energy. Breaking a nucleus into its nucleons also needs energy.
quiz.3.q: A nucleus X emits first one alpha and then two beta minus particles in a row, turning into nucleus Y. Which is true for Y?
quiz.3.o.0: Its mass number is the same as X's
quiz.3.o.1: Its atomic number is 2 less than X's
quiz.3.o.2: It is an isobar of X
quiz.3.o.3: It is an isotope of X
quiz.3.e: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. Two beta minus emissions raise Z by 2. In the end Z stays the same and A goes down by 4. Since the element is the same and the mass number is different, the new nucleus is an isotope.
quiz.3.y.0: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4. Beta emissions do not change it. So in total the mass number goes down by 4.
quiz.3.y.1: Alpha emission lowers the atomic number by 2, and two beta minus emissions raise it by 2. So the atomic number does not change.
quiz.3.y.2: An isobar is a nucleus with the same mass number. Since alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4, no isobar forms.
A:ozet: Build a nucleus and make an isotope. Weigh the strong force, see the mass defect on a balance and find the most stable nucleus. Go from uranium down to lead, separate the radiations, calculate a half-life and control a chain reaction.
A:adimlar.0.metin: This is a carbon-12 nucleus. Turn it into carbon-14.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: The nucleus has 6 protons and 8 neutrons: 146C. Since Z stayed the same, this is still carbon, and only A changed. So this is an isotope of carbon.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.ipucu: The number of protons decides the element, and for carbon Z must stay 6. Change the number of neutrons to make A = 14.
A:adimlar.1.metin: The protons in a nucleus repel each other electrically. The strong nuclear force holds them together. Move the two protons apart (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m) and watch how the two forces change.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: Which is true for the strong nuclear force?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The strong force does not depend on charge. It also acts between a proton and a neutron and between two neutrons.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: It falls off more slowly with distance than electric repulsion
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: It is the other way around. On the graph the green curve dies out much faster than the red one. At a few fm the strong attraction is almost zero.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: It has a very short range
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: At about 1 fm the strong attraction easily beats the repulsion. At a few fm it drops almost to zero. This is why the nucleus is so small.
A:adimlar.2.metin: One pan of the balance holds 2 protons and 2 neutrons, all separate. The other pan holds the helium-4 nucleus they form when they join. The parts in the two pans are the same.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Which side of the balance is heavier?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The nucleus is lighter than its parts. The missing mass was released as energy when the nucleus formed.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Mass does not increase when the parts join. On the contrary, part of the mass turns into energy and is released.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The parts are the same, but the masses are not equal. The difference is called the mass defect.
A:adimlar.3.metin: If you divide the binding energy by the nucleon number, you see how tightly a nucleus is bound. Change the mass number and find the peak of the curve.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: The peak is around A ≈ 56-62, where the energy per nucleon is about 8.8 MeV. Iron-56 and nickel-62 are among the most stable nuclei.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: The curve rises fast for light nuclei and falls slowly for heavy ones. Look for the highest point in between.
A:adimlar.4.metin: α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ decay raises Z by 1. <sup>238</sup>U decays step by step down to stable <sup>206</sup>Pb. How many α and how many β⁻ does this take?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The difference in A is 238 − 206 = 32. Since only α changes A, it takes 32 / 4 = 8 α. 8 α lower Z by 16, down to 76. For Z to rise to 82, it takes 6 β⁻.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: First find the number of α from the difference in A: 238 − 206 = 32. Then fix Z with β⁻.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A source gives off α, β⁻ and γ radiation. The radiations will pass first between two charged plates, then through sheets of paper, aluminum and lead.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which is deflected most in the electric field?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: α has a double charge, but it is very heavy, because it is a helium nucleus. So it bends only a little toward the negative plate.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: β⁻ is an electron. Its charge-to-mass ratio is thousands of times that of α, so it bends the most, toward the positive plate. Uncharged γ does not bend at all.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: γ is an uncharged photon. So it does not bend at all in an electric field.
A:adimlar.6.metin: How long must you wait for 15 g to be left from 120 g of a substance with a half-life of 4 days?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: The amount goes from 120 to 60, to 30 and to 15. That is three half-lives, or 12 days.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.ipucu: How many times must you halve 120 to get 15? Each halving takes 4 days.
A:adimlar.7.metin: In a power plant, control rods absorb the extra neutrons. How many neutrons from each fission must cause a new fission for the reaction to go on at a steady rate?
A:adimlar.7.gorev.tamam: If each fission starts exactly one new fission, the reaction goes on at a steady rate. This is how nuclear power plants work. If the number is 2 or 3, the number of fissions multiplies with each generation and the reaction gets out of control. If it is 0, the reaction dies out.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.ipucu: The number of fissions must stay the same from one generation to the next.
A:kapanis.0: Z is the number of protons and decides the element. A = Z + N. Nuclei with the same Z but different A are called isotopes.
A:kapanis.1: The strong nuclear force does not depend on charge and has a very short range.
A:kapanis.2: A nucleus is lighter than its parts, and the difference corresponds to an energy of E = Δm·c². Binding energy per nucleon is greatest around iron.
A:kapanis.3: α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ raises Z by 1, and β⁺ lowers Z by 1. In γ emission A and Z do not change.
A:kapanis.4: In an electric field β⁻ is deflected most, and γ is not deflected. The order of penetration is γ > β > α.
A:kapanis.5: The amount left is found with N = N₀ / 2ⁿ. Fission splits a nucleus, and fusion joins nuclei. Both release energy.
